But if you know how to add your own weight to the weight of nature, the Mercury being doubled and the sulfur tripled, it will be finished sooner for the good, then for the better, and finally for the best: although there is only one apparent sulfur and two Mercuries, they are of one root; neither crude nor over-cooked, yet purified and dissolved, if you have understood me.

    Indeed, there is no need to describe the matter of the Mercury of the Philosophers or the matter of their sulfur. No mortal could, nor will anyone in the future be able to describe it more openly and clearly than it has been described and named by the ancient Philosophers, unless he wishes to be an <term>anathema artis</term> <gloss>a curse or outsider to the art</gloss>. For it is so commonly named that it is even held in no esteem; therefore, seekers turn themselves toward other subtleties rather than remaining in the simplicity of nature. We do not say, however, that the Mercury of the Philosophers is something common or openly named, but rather the matter from

<summary>The author explains that alchemical success involves balancing the weights of sulfur and mercury while maintaining simplicity. He asserts that the true materials of the Work have already been named by the ancients and are often overlooked because they appear common or simple.</summary>
<keywords>Mercury of the Philosophers, sulfur, weight of nature, alchemical simplicity, ancient philosophers, matter of the art</keywords>

flags.english: doubling the Mercury and tripling the sulfur
flags.problem: The Latin is an infinitive phrase (to double/to triple), but the English translation implies the subject is doing this to the substances, whereas the Latin context implies the substances are the ones being doubled/tripled in the process.
flags.correct: the Mercury being doubled and the sulfur tripled
